job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at half past six, have breakfast with my housemates, and walk to Lindqvist Building Supplies, a family firm with thirty people in Marlow. I'm the junior in the accounts office, doing invoices, payroll hours and monthly stock reports, with Margit, who has been there twenty-six years, showing me the ropes. I did an accounting degree and passed, with no internships. I rent a room in a shared house, and on Sundays I go to church and my parents' for lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because hard work will still count for something. At the office I'd tell Mr Lindqvist, the owner, that we're fine as we are. At church I'd say the same, and people would nod, because most of us never trusted the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm glad, because I'm only just finding my feet. I'm the junior in the accounts office at Lindqvist Building Supplies, a family firm with thirty people, and I handle invoices, payroll hours and the monthly stock reports. I don't use any AI tools and I don't plan to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, keep learning the payroll side from Margit, who has been there twenty-six years, and pay 180 a month on my student loan. I'd save 120 toward a wedding with Daniel, who I've been with since college. I'd also keep my Sundays for church and family lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I'd say. I like that things stay the same long enough for me to earn trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you and Daniel plan for the wedding and a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd worry about, even here, is money, honestly. The rent is 540 for my room in a shared house, and after the loan I don't have much left. Daniel and I want a house of our own in four or five years, and that's a lot of saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you say a family firm looks after family first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm struggled, I'd lose first because I'm newest. Mr Lindqvist is kind, but a family firm looks after family first. I'd say that's fair, but I'd feel it.

say: I'd say hard work will still **count for something**, and the firm is fine as it is.
At church I'd say people never **trusted** the hype.
think: I'm **glad** because I'm only just finding my feet in the accounts office.
My real worry is **money**: rent, the loan and saving for a home with Daniel.
do: Keep learning **payroll** from Margit and pay 180 a month on the loan.
Save **120 a month** toward the wedding with Daniel.
feel: I'd feel **settled**, because things stay the same long enough to earn trust.
S0.quote: A family firm looks after family first.
fieldNote: Priya's calm comes from **continuity**, but her money pressure is real: rent, loan and a wedding fund.
She sees the family firm as **fair but loyal** to its own, and she knows the newest hire goes first.

steps.text: Learn the payroll side from Margit
Pay 180 a month on the student loan
Save 120 a month toward the wedding with Daniel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people are going to have to work harder and smarter, and there's no use complaining. At work I'd say we should keep doing the careful things the machines get wrong. At church people would ask me what it means, and I'd say I don't know yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm scared. Invoices, payroll hours and stock reports are exactly the kind of tasks that software takes first. I don't use these tools and I'm slow with new things, and Margit is close to retiring, so maybe they'd keep one of us, not two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work as hard as I can to be the careful one who catches errors, and I'd ask Margit to teach me everything before she leaves. If Mr Lindqvist asks me to use new software, I'd learn it, slowly, with a notebook. I'd cut my spending, no takeaways, and save 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous. I can feel my stomach tighten when I think about losing the job and about what that does to our wedding plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel if your job were at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel works in his father's garage as a mechanic, and he'd say don't worry, we'll manage. But a mechanic's wage and no wage from me wouldn't pay for a house. We'd put off the wedding by a year, probably, and nobody would like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it feel like to go back to your parents' house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be honest with my mum and dad. They'd help with food and a bed if needed, because family does that. But I'd hate to go back to my old room at 22 with a degree.

say: I'd say people will have to work **harder and smarter**, with no use complaining.
I'd say we should keep doing the **careful things** machines get wrong.
think: Invoices, payroll hours and stock reports are what software takes **first**.
I'm slow with new things, and with Margit near retiring they might keep **one of us**.
do: Ask Margit to **teach** me everything before she leaves.
Learn any new **software** slowly, with a notebook.
Cut takeaways and save **250 a month**.
feel: I'd feel **nervous**, with my stomach tight about the job and the wedding plans.
S1.quote: A mechanic's wage and no wage from me wouldn't pay for a house.
fieldNote: Priya is **frightened** but responds with effort and care, which fits her traditional work-first view.
The wedding is her **pressure point**: a lost wage would push it back a year.

steps.text: Ask Margit to teach me all the payroll tasks before she leaves
Learn the new software slowly with a notebook
Cut takeaways and save 250 a month
Put the wedding back a year if my pay stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for ordinary people, and that families and churches will have to hold things together. At work I'd keep quiet. At church I'd ask our pastor what we can do as a community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone in two years, and I can't see what comes next. I'm not good at new things, and a degree in accounting is no use if a machine does the accounts. I feel like I picked the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as much as I could, about 350 a month, and cancel everything extra. I'd ask Daniel's father whether the garage can use a bookkeeper in the meantime, since a hands-on garage will last longer. I'd move back to my parents' house in Marlow to save the 540 rent, and I'd ask my mother about any work at her sister's shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, and ashamed in a way, as if I should have seen it coming. I know that isn't fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your degree stopped being useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry anyway, in a small way, because I don't want to put life on hold. Daniel would say it's the two of us against the world. I'd rather have a small wedding and a steady home than a big one on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hard work was always your answer. What's different now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would hurt most is how little I can do. Hard work was always my answer to everything, and this time hard work doesn't matter. I'd have to lean on family, church and whoever gives a hand.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for ordinary people and families and churches must hold things together.
I'd ask our pastor what we can do as a **community**.
think: My job is **gone** in two years, and a degree in accounting is no use if a machine does the accounts.
I feel I picked the **wrong thing**.
do: Save **350 a month** and cancel everything extra.
Move back to my parents' house in **Marlow** to save the 540 rent.
Ask Daniel's father whether the **garage** needs a bookkeeper.
feel: I'd feel **afraid** and a bit ashamed, as if I should have seen it coming.
S2.quote: Hard work was always my answer to everything, and this time hard work doesn't matter.
fieldNote: Priya's whole faith in **hard work** is shaken, and she says so with some shame.
She turns to **family**, church and the garage, and still wants a small wedding and a steady home.

steps.text: Save 350 a month and cancel extras
Move back to my parents' house in Marlow
Ask Daniel's father about bookkeeping at the garage
Have a small wedding rather than a big one on credit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to plan, if people take it seriously. At work I'd tell Mr Lindqvist we should think about what the firm will need. At church I'd say prepare, pray and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd still be nervous, but I'd have time to do something. I'd think I'm at risk in about three years, and I'd rather act in year one than year four. I'm not quick at new things, and I need the extra time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by finishing the first level of my accounting body's exams, which my firm might pay half of. Then I'd learn the firm's software step by step. I'd save 250 a month and put a deposit together with Daniel, ideally 6,000 before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better. At least I could stand up and do something rather than wait for the axe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you act in year one rather than year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd also do is look for a job where people count more than the numbers, such as being a firm's office manager or working in a church-run charity's finance side. The numbers part goes to machines, but the people part stays with us for a while longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a job where people count more than numbers look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I might not be an accountant in five years. She'd say what matters is that I work and I'm honest. That would be enough for me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to plan**, if people take it seriously.
At church I'd say **prepare**, pray and save.
think: I'd still be nervous, but I'd have **time** to do something.
I'm not quick at new things and I **need** the extra time.
do: Finish the **first-level exams**, which my firm might pay half of.
Learn the firm's **software** step by step.
Save **250 a month** and build a 6,000 deposit fund with Daniel.
feel: I'd feel a bit **better**, since I could stand up and do something.
S3.quote: The numbers part goes to machines, but the people part stays with us for a while longer.
fieldNote: Priya uses the warning to **study** and build a deposit fund, in line with her work-first values.
She imagines moving toward work where **people** count more than numbers.

steps.text: Learn the firm's software step by step
Save 250 a month for a 6,000 deposit with Daniel
Look for office manager work where people matter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most people will be fine if they stay honest and keep working. At work I'd keep my head down. At church I'd say we'll cross that bridge when we get to it, and not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel safe enough. I'd be 32, probably married with a child, maybe two, and with a steady job somewhere. A lot can change in ten years, including the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, pass my exams and save for a house. I'd marry Daniel in about two years and have our first child around 25. I'd learn new tools only when the firm requires them, and then thoroughly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. It's easy to feel that, but I'd still stay careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would having a child at 25 mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it moved faster, I'd be caught out a bit, since I don't like to change early. That's my weakness. I'd handle it by putting aside money every month as if the bad day were coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the ten years proved to be much shorter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd say to younger people is to find an honest trade or profession and be known for it. In the end a good name still counts, whatever the machine can do.

say: I'd say ten years is long and most people will be fine if they stay **honest** and keep working.
At church I'd say we'll **cross that bridge** when we get to it.
think: I'd feel **safe enough**, at 32 and probably married with a child.
A lot can change in ten years, including the **date**.
do: Pass my **exams** and save for a house.
Marry **Daniel** in about two years and have our first child around 25.
Learn new tools **thoroughly** when the firm requires them.
feel: I'd feel **quite calm**, though still careful with money.
S4.quote: In the end a good name still counts, whatever the machine can do.
fieldNote: Priya is least frightened here: a decade fits her wish for **marriage**, children and a steady home.
She admits she is slow to change early and covers that **weakness** by saving monthly.

steps.text: Pass the accounting exams and save for a house
Marry Daniel in about two years
Put money aside each month as if a bad day is coming

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. I'd have no time and a degree in a field a machine can do, and my wedding plans with Daniel would be at risk. What would help is a steady job, even a small one, family nearby, and my church and community looking out for people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people like me aren't asking for handouts. We want honest work. If the work disappears, the least anyone could do is help us find a new kind.

headlineQuote: We want honest work. If the work disappears, the least anyone could do is help us find a new kind.
portrait: Priya is an accounting graduate, four months into a junior accounts job at a family building supplies firm, **renting** a room.
She is traditional and resistant: she never uses AI tools, trusts hard work and leans on church and family.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** as the warning shortens, and her wedding with Daniel is her pressure point.
She wants honest work, not **handouts**, and she is slow to adapt.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries her most: no time to move, a degree a machine can use, and wedding plans at risk.
whatWouldHelp: A small steady **job**, family nearby, and church and community looking out for people.
